question.problem: Find the inverse of the function $f(x)=\frac{1}{4\sqrt[3]{x}}+2.$
question.worked_solution:
To find ${f}^{-1}(x),$ we start by replacing $f(x)$ with $y:$

$$
y=\frac{1}{4\sqrt[3]{x}}+2
$$

Now, interchanging $x$ and $y$ gives

$$
x=\frac{1}{4\sqrt[3]{y}}+2.
$$

Then, we make $y$ the subject of the equation as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt[3]{y}}+2 \\ x-2 & =\frac{1}{4\sqrt[3]{y}} \\ \sqrt[3]{y} & =\frac{1}{4(x-2)} \\ (\sqrt[3]{y})^{3} & ={(\frac{1}{4(x-2)})}^{3} \\ y & =\frac{1}{64(x-2)^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the inverse function is 

$$
{f}^{-1}(x)=\frac{1}{64(x-2)^{3}}.
$$

**Note**: The domain and range of $f(x)$ are

$$
x\ne 0,\,f(x)\ne 2.
$$

Therefore, the domain and range of ${f}^{-1}(x)$ are

$$
x\ne 2,\,{f}^{-1}(x)\ne 0.
$$
